title: Chapter 28: The Morning Dew 1
content:
Chapter 28

The Morning Dew 1

Passing through the city gates, the two walked shoulder to shoulder into the bustling crowd. Without warning, Lan Wangji broke the silence. "How is the curse mark?"

"Jin Ling was buried way too close to our dear friend back there," Wei Wuxian said casually. "Soaked up a ton of resentment. It’s faded a bit, but it’s still lingering. We’ll probably have to track down the rest of the corpse—or at least the head—before we can wipe it out completely. Nothing to lose sleep over."

'Dear friend' was their affectionate placeholder for the poor soul who had been drawn and quartered. Since they had no clue who the guy actually was, Wei Wuxian had tossed out the nickname. Lan Wangji hadn't said a word when he first heard it, but he hadn't objected either, which was as good as tacit approval. Naturally, Hanguang-jun himself would never let the phrase cross his lips.

"How much is 'a bit'?" Lan Wangji asked.

Wei Wuxian held up two fingers, pinching a minuscule gap between them. "A bit is a bit. What, want me to strip down and show you?"

Lan Wangji’s brow gave a faint twitch, as if genuinely concerned the man might drop his trousers in broad daylight. "Wait until we are back," he replied, his tone as flat as ever.

Wei Wuxian burst into a laugh, spinning around on his heel to walk backward ahead of him. Earlier on, desperate to slip Lan Wangji's grip, he’d played the fool to the absolute limit—acting shamelessly unhinged and thoroughly humiliating himself. If anyone else had their cover blown like this, the sheer shame of looking back on those antics would make them want to dig a hole and crawl inside. But Wei Wuxian’s skin had always been forged from steel, so he simply carried on like nothing had happened. Then again, anyone with an ounce of self-respect wouldn't have pulled stunts like crawling into someone's bedroll in the dead of night, trying to muscle their way into the same bath barrel, or batting heavily painted eyelashes while asking if they looked pretty. Since he was playing dumb and acting like none of it had ever occurred, Lan Wangji naturally wouldn't bring it up either. They simply pretended the past few days hadn't happened.

This was the first time since his cover was blown that Wei Wuxian had dared to crack another joke like that.

Letting the laughter fade, his expression smoothed out into serious focus. "Hanguang-jun, what do you think? The person who dumped our dear friend's arm in Mo Village to ambush your juniors, and the person who stitched his legs onto another corpse and buried him in that wall—are they the same party?"

Though he’d always called Lan Wangji by his birth name in the past—and still did in his own head—he’d spent the last few weeks tossing the formal title around until it had become muscle memory. Besides, hearing himself say it carried a kind of deadpan, theatrical mock-seriousness that amused him, so he kept using it out in public.

"Two different parties," Lan Wangji answered.

"Great minds think alike," Wei Wuxian agreed. "Going through all the trouble of grafting his legs onto another corpse and stuffing them into a double-layered wall means they were desperate to keep those parts hidden. If that’s their goal, why turn around and chuck the left arm straight at the Gusu Lan Clan? That's practically begging for an investigation. One took painstaking measures to hide the remains, while the other recklessly lobbed a limb into the open, terrified nobody would notice. Definitely not the same person."

Having had his entire line of thought articulated for him, Lan Wangji had little left to add. He settled for a low, affirming, "Mn."

Wei Wuxian turned back around, matching his stride. "Whoever hid the legs knew all about the Qinghe Nie Clan’s blade pavilion, and whoever threw the left arm had an eye on your clan's movements. Neither of them is an amateur. The plot thickens."

"One step at a time," Lan Wangji said.

"So, how did you recognize me?" Wei Wuxian asked, pivoting on a dime.

"Figure it out yourself."

They had been volleying back and forth without missing a beat, and Wei Wuxian had hoped to catch him off-guard and trick him into spilling the answer. Thwarted once again, he didn't lose heart, changing the subject without a breath. "I’ve never set foot in Yueyang before. I was the one asking around last time, so I’m taking a break today. Care to do the legwork, Hanguang-jun? Mind lending a hand?"

Lan Wangji didn't hesitate, turning on his heel to head down the street.

Wei Wuxian called after him immediately, "Hold on! Where are you going, Hanguang-jun?"

Lan Wangji glanced back. "To seek the local cultivation sect."

Catching the silk tassel of Bichen's hilt, Wei Wuxian reeled him right back. "What for? This is their turf. Even if they knew something, they wouldn't breathe a word to you. If it’s a mess they can't handle, they'll bury it out of sheer embarrassment; if they think they can manage, their pride won't let them accept outside help. My esteemed Hanguang-jun, I'm not trying to run your name through the mud, but you really can't get things done without me out here. If you manage to squeeze any useful dirt out of a local clan with that approach, it'll be a miracle."

The jab was entirely blunt, but beneath Lan Wangji’s lowered lashes, his gaze remained quiet and soft. "Mn," he hummed softly.

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "'Mn'? What's with the 'mn'? You're agreeing to that too?" Inwardly, he shook his head with fond amusement: Still nothing but 'mn'—as stiff as ever!

"Then how should we inquire?" Lan Wangji asked.

Wei Wuxian pointed a finger. "Over there, obviously."

He was aiming toward a wide thoroughfare lined on both sides with high, fluttering banners dyed a vibrant, eye-catching crimson. Every storefront sat wide open, with rows of plump, pitch-black liquor jars spilling from the thresholds straight out onto the pavement. Shop hands milled about, carrying trays of shallow drinking bowls, eagerly pitching their wares to every passerby.

The rich, heady aroma of fermented grain blanketed the entire street. No wonder Wei Wuxian’s footsteps had slowed to a crawl earlier, grinding to a dead halt the moment he hit the corner—and dragging Lan Wangji along with him.

Putting on his most upright, serious face, Wei Wuxian argued, "The hands working these stalls are usually young, sharp, and quick on their feet. Places like this see constant foot traffic from morning till night, meaning endless chatter. If there's any bizarre rumor drifting around the region, you can bet it passes through their ears first."

Lan Wangji didn't object, offering another quiet "Mn," though his face practically had You just want a drinkwritten across it in bold ink.

Wei Wuxian feigned complete ignorance. Keeping his grip firmly on Bichen’s sword tassel, his eyes lit up as he dragged the man straight into the wine district. Half a dozen shop boys swarmed them in an instant, their pitches colliding over one another: "Care for a sip, Young Master? He Family Brew, the pride of the city!"

"Try a taste here, sir! Samples are free of charge—if it hits the spot, you can sit down for a jar!"

"It might smell mellow, but trust me, it packs a mule's kick once it hits your belly!"

"If you're still standing after a bowl, I'll take your family name!"

Hearing that, Wei Wuxian perked up. "Deal!"

He took the bowl from the boy's tray, tipped his head back, and drained it clean in one smooth gulp. Flipping the bowl upside down with a grin, he showed off the dry glaze. "Taking my name, are you?"

The shop boy didn't flinch. Raising his chin, he doubled down with twice the bravado: "I said after a whole jar!"

Wei Wuxian beamed. "Then bring me three."

Overjoyed, the boy spun around and sprinted into the shop. Turning back to Lan Wangji, Wei Wuxian said, "That’s how business works: patronize them first, talk later. Grease the wheels, and their lips loosen right up."

Lan Wangji reached into his robes and footed the bill.

They stepped inside, settling at one of the wooden tables meant for patrons to rest and chat over their drinks. Another shop hand took one look at Lan Wangji’s ethereal bearing and noble silks, immediately treating him like a visiting immortal; he wiped down the bench and tabletop three times over before daring to invite them to sit.

With two jars resting by his boots and one held firmly in his grip, Wei Wuxian traded a couple of breezy pleasantries with the boy before steering the conversation toward local oddities. The server loved to talk, rubbing his palms eagerly. "What kind of strange things are we talking about?"

"Haunted estates, desecrated graves, severed corpses—that sort of thing."

The boy’s eyes darted between them. "Oh... What do you two do, exactly?"

"Haven't you already figured that out?" Wei Wuxian teased.

"Right, right," the server grinned knowingly. "Easy to spot. You gentlemen must be from one of those sects that fly on swords and glide on the clouds. Especially your friend here—in all my days, I’ve never laid eyes on a man so... so..."

"So handsome?" Wei Wuxian supplied with a chuckle.

The boy laughed. "Careful, sir, you might offend him talking like that! But as for bizarre happenings? We've got one. Not from recent days, mind you—it went down about ten years back. Head out of the city gates that way, walk about two or three li, and you’ll run into a rather grand estate. Not sure if their family plaque is still hanging, but folks around here call it the Chang Residence."

Wei Wuxian’s interest piqued. "What happened to the estate?"

"A total massacre!" the boy whispered, leaning in. "You asked for the strangest story in town, so I’m giving you the worst of the worst. The entire clan was wiped out in a single night. And word has it... every single one of them was literally scared to death!"

Hearing that, Lan Wangji’s gaze shifted, looking thoughtful, as though an old memory had been stirred. Wei Wuxian didn't notice, pressing on: "Is there an established cultivation clan overseeing this region?"

To scare an entire household to death in one night pointed toward a vicious, extraordinarily lethal spirit. Not every clan carried the complicated baggage of the Qinghe Nie Clan; ordinary sects wouldn't tolerate a horror like that running loose in their territory.

"There was," the boy answered. "Of course there was."

"How did they handle it back then?"

"Handle it?" The server tossed his wiping cloth over his shoulder and pulled up a stool, finally dropping the punchline he’d been sitting on. "Young Master, do you know the family name of the sect that used to oversee Yueyang? Chang. The very family that was slaughtered! Every last soul was wiped out—who was left to handle it?"

The annihilated Chang Clan was the local cultivation sect?!

Wei Wuxian had never heard of the Yueyang Chang Clan, meaning it was likely a minor household rather than a prominent powerhouse, but the complete eradication of an entire sect was a massive, horrific disaster.

He leaned in closer. "How were they wiped out?"

"Just going off what folks say, mind you," the boy said, lowering his voice. "One night, a frantic pounding started hammering against the front gates of the Chang estate."

Wei Wuxian echoed, "Pounding?"

"Yes! Loud enough to shake the sky! Screaming, sobbing, howling from inside—like the whole household was locked in and couldn't get out. Strange, right? Gates are bolted from the inside. If you want to leave your own house, you just slide the bolt back and walk out. Why beat on the wood like that? It’s not like anyone outside could unlatch it for them. And if the doors wouldn't budge, why not vault the perimeter walls?"

The boy shook his head, caught up in the drama. "The neighbors listening in the dark were thoroughly creeped out. Everyone knew the Chang Clan was a prestigious cultivation family around these parts. Their master—Chang Ping, I think his name was—had a flying sword! A real flying sword he could stand on! If something went down that even their masters couldn't handle, an ordinary mortal poking their nose in would just be begging for an early grave. So nobody dared bring a ladder or peek over the walls. The screaming went on all through the night, getting weaker and weaker until dawn. Then, the moment the sun crested the horizon, the main gates swung open all on their own.

"The entire courtyard... over a dozen masters and mistresses, more than fifty servants, slumped across chairs, sprawled on the ground, bile pooling around their mouths. Every last one of them was frightened to death."

From behind the counter, the shopkeeper barked across the room, "Look at you slacking off! Who asked you to rattle on about old corpses instead of working?!"

Wei Wuxian called out smoothly, "Bring us five more jars."

Lan Wangji dropped enough silver on the counter to cover ten.

The shopkeeper’s scowl vanished into an instant, beaming smile. He turned to the server, waving a hand. "Take good care of our guests! Don't go wandering off!"

Wei Wuxian turned back to the boy. "Go on."

With his boss bought off, the server threw himself into the storytelling, pitching his voice to a dramatic cadence: "For a long time after that, if you walked near the Chang estate after dark, you could still hear that pounding against the timber!

"Think about it: people who cultivate immortality, who fly on swords and fight monsters for a living, had seen plenty of ghouls—yet they were scared to death. How horrifying would that thing have to be? Walk down enough dark alleys, and you're bound to bump into a ghost. People swear they could even hear pounding coming from inside the coffins after they were buried! Even though the clan leader, Chang Ping, happened to be away on business and dodged the blade..."

Wei Wuxian interrupted, "Didn't you just say the entire family was wiped out?"
